meta.headline_end_year_note: 2031-32 is past the OBR March 2026 forecast, so it uses policyengine-uk's long-run assumptions (CPI 2.0%, earnings growth 3.3%).
meta.cpi_ahc_note: CPI after housing costs, used for real incomes after housing costs, is a PolicyEngine derivation, not an OBR forecast. With the corrected index in policyengine-uk#2531, real growth after housing costs from 2027-28 to 2031-32 would be higher by less than 0.1 points, for the median and every decile. No poverty rate uses it.

method.mean_equivalised_income: Person-weighted mean of equiv_hbai_household_net_income (BHC, modified OECD scale, household weight x household_count_people), as in HBAI
method.median_equivalised_income: Person-weighted median of equiv_hbai_household_net_income (BHC), as in HBAI
method.mean_equivalised_income_ahc: Person-weighted mean of equiv_hbai_household_net_income_ahc, as in HBAI
method.median_equivalised_income_ahc: Person-weighted median of equiv_hbai_household_net_income_ahc, as in HBAI
method.income_outturn: HBAI Table 1.2b (£ per week in 2024/25 prices) x 52, rebased to 2027-28 prices; BHC cash values recovered with the OBR CPI index; AHC outturn is real only (nominal null)
method.poverty: Person-weighted share of people in households with in_poverty_bhc / in_poverty_ahc (absolute, 60% of FYE 2025 median held in real terms) and in_relative_poverty_bhc / in_relative_poverty_ahc (60% of contemporary median)
method.groups: hbai_person_type: HBAI dependent children (is_hbai_dependent_child), working-age adults below State Pension age, and pensioners at or above it; each person in exactly one group
method.income_by_decile: Person-weighted deciles of equiv_hbai_household_net_income (BHC) and _ahc (AHC), re-ranked each year; decile medians deflated by CPI (BHC) or CPI-AHC (AHC)
method.non_pensioner_split: People in benefit units with no hbai_person_type PENSIONER member, split at their own median AHC income; mean AHC income of each half
method.child_poverty_by_family: Children (hbai_person_type CHILD) by the count of is_hbai_dependent_child in their benefit unit and by adults in it (members who are not dependent children: 1 = lone parent, 2+ = couple)
method.inequality: Person-weighted Gini (incomes as computed, negatives kept) and p90/p10 of equivalised BHC and AHC income
method.deep_poverty: Share of people with equivalised AHC income below 40% and 50% of the person-weighted median AHC income in the same year
method.poverty_by_group: tenure_type (council and housing association combined as social rent), benefit-unit family type, and region; unweighted counts are distinct households in the cell
method.obr_rhdi: Table 1.5 (Per person), By total population: Real household disposable income, columns D (index, 2008Q1=100) and G (£ thousands, 2023 prices), fiscal-year rows (RHDI (chained volume measure, ONS NRJR) divided by total population (ONS EBAQ))

comparators.child_poverty: DWP, Low income poverty projections for children, FYE 2026 to FYE 2031 (July 2026)

notes: Model projections; not yet validated against outturn.
Income outturn is HBAI, published in real terms; BHC cash values are recovered with OBR CPI, and AHC outturn is shown in real terms only.
Poverty and inequality outturn is the HBAI admin-linked series, which starts in 2021-22.
The 2024-25 model point uses the weights solved for 2025, scaled for population, so it carries 2025 composition and caseloads (UC £74bn).
OBR series are calendar years; CPI after housing costs and social rent are PolicyEngine derivations, not OBR forecasts.
Until a later OBR forecast is loaded, the post series repeat the March 2026 forecast.
caveats: Ages and benefit take-up are held fixed, so the State Pension age rise to 67 removes State Pension from 66-year-olds with no work response.
The population is uprated uniformly, so its age structure stays as in 2025.
Results for small groups are noisy: calibration roughly halves the effective sample, so family-size figures are approximate.
The September 2026 free school meals expansion to all Universal Credit families in England is not modelled, so child poverty from 2026-27 is a little high.
The Universal Credit health element is assigned too widely (through disabled children, and twice to some couples), so child poverty is a little low.
The above-inflation rises in the Universal Credit standard allowance from 2027-28 are missing, so UC is about £0.6bn too low by 2029-30.

notes: The absolute line is the official one: 60% of the 2024-25 HBAI median (£431.69 a week before housing costs for a couple), uprated by CPI. Our 2024-25 incomes are higher than in HBAI at the bottom and middle of the distribution (median about 1% higher), so absolute and relative poverty both sit below official figures. On the same survey records with the survey's own weights the model reproduces the HBAI median and poverty rates; the difference comes from reweighting the data to 2025 administrative totals. Read the projections as changes from 2024-25.

groups.above_middle: Non-pensioners at or above the non-pensioner median

notes: Deciles are re-ranked each year, so growth compares the same position in the distribution, not the same people.

The lowest tenth's median after housing costs is the 5th percentile, a noisy point, and its fall sits in the bottom 5%. To 2029-30 the main drivers were the State Pension age rise to 67 on a dataset whose ages are held fixed and Local Housing Allowance frozen beyond 2026-27; later years are not decomposed.
The halves are split at the non-pensioner median and show means, not medians.

groups.three_plus_children: Three or more children in family

notes: Outturn is HBAI Table 1.2b: Gini, and the ratio of top to bottom quintile medians, which is the 90th over the 10th percentile.

Read the projection as a change, not a level. Our Gini is about 2.1 points below official figures in 2024-25 before housing costs (2.0 after). Our data have fewer very low incomes, and we treat very high incomes differently from the SPI-based adjustment in HBAI. The 90:10 ratio is low (3.49 against 3.71 before housing costs, 4.17 against 4.54 after) because the bottom tenth is too high, not because the top is too low.

measures.below_40pc_median_ahc: Very deep poverty: below 40% of median income (AHC)

notes: Lines are 40% and 50% of the model's own median equivalised AHC income each year.
Not the model's in_deep_poverty_ahc flag, which is half the absolute poverty line.
Our very deep poverty (7.8%, 5.4 million in 2027-28) is below published estimates on the older survey series, so read it as a change, not a level.

measures.median_equivalised_income_bhc: Median equivalised income (BHC), £ a year, adjusted for household size (shown for a couple with no children)

notes: Cells with fewer than 100 unweighted households are suppressed (null); none are at this sample size.
Family type is at benefit-unit level; a pensioner family is any benefit unit with someone at or above State Pension age.
Region: model estimates, not validated against official regional figures (Northern Ireland is far above DfC's own figure); not shown on the page.

income_growth_by_group.method: Each population is ranked on its own equivalised income (BHC on BHC income, AHC on AHC income), re-ranked each year, and cut into person-weighted groups; each group's median is deflated by CPI (BHC) or CPI-AHC (AHC). annual_growth is the change on the year before (for 2027-28, on 2026-27); cumulative_growth the change since 2027-28.
